frameworks.name: More, Better, New Scaling
frameworks.definition: Three-stage decision hierarchy for growth: exhaust more volume on the current thing, then optimize what you have, only then switch to something different (new).

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when two customer segments differ in average order value by approximately 25-100x, targeting the higher-value segment is preferable even though it produces more unqualified leads, because the absolute profit from the good accounts in the higher segment exceeds the total profit available from the lower-value segment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Middleman or reseller business model where operational effort per order is roughly equal regardless of order size
Higher-value segment order size is 25x or more above lower-value segment
claims.mechanism: When operational cost per order is essentially fixed, absolute gross profit per order is the only variable that scales with order size; a 25-100x difference in order value overwhelms any reasonable difference in qualification rate.

numbers.axis: annual spend per customer by segment (custom apparel business, 2024)

bounded_by: Does not apply when the higher-value segment has fundamentally different operational requirements (would require relearning delivery from scratch)
Does not apply when the lower-value segment has proven compounding retention that would stack into a monopoly position over time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that identifying customer data (who buys, who retains, what segment characteristics predict high lifetime value) is the first and most important task in a business because it governs offer design, channel selection, and messaging; delaying this data collection delays leverage on every downstream decision.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business that has not yet identified which customer segments produce high LTV
Business with multiple heterogeneous customer segments
claims.mechanism: Customer identity determines offer design, which determines channel choice, which determines messaging; errors at the customer-selection layer compound through every downstream decision, so fixing it first produces the greatest leverage.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that absolute gross profit per order (not gross margin percentage) is the correct north-star metric for a middleman or reseller business, because a large order at lower margin percentage produces more absolute dollars with the same operational effort as a small order at higher margin percentage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Middleman or outsourced manufacturing business where per-unit operational cost scales with volume but founder/overhead cost does not
claims.mechanism: Middlemen add value in design and coordination; those costs are roughly fixed per order regardless of order size, so margin percentage understates the value of large-volume orders versus small-volume orders.

numbers.axis: absolute gross profit comparison between order types (illustrative, McKenzie's custom apparel business)

bounded_by: Does not apply when larger orders require proportionally more operational overhead (e.g., custom manufacturing, not outsourced middleman)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the More/Better/New hierarchy (do more of current thing first, then better, only then different) has an exception: when a new customer segment offers approximately 100x the order value with no change in operational effort, switching to the new segment is justified before exhausting the current one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: New target segment produces ~100x order value vs. current segment
Operational delivery process is identical or nearly identical between segments
Current market cannot absorb 10-50x volume increase without fundamental model changes
claims.mechanism: The opportunity cost of not pursuing the higher-value segment grows as the multiplier increases; at 100x the normal 'do more first' heuristic is overridden because the downside of staying small vastly exceeds the downside of a failed pivot.

numbers.axis: order value multiplier threshold that justifies breaking More/Better/New rule

anchors.value: stick with current channel, do more volume

anchors.region: ~100x order value difference (50 shirts vs 5,000 shirts)
anchors.value: justified to switch to new segment first

bounded_by: Does not apply if the new segment requires fundamentally different delivery (relearning the business)
Does not apply if the new segment has no proven revenue retention potential

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a lower-value customer segment has very low churn and compounding retention, the correct growth strategy within that segment is increasing order frequency (more orders per year per customer) rather than switching to a higher-value segment — but this path is only viable if the goal is moderate revenue growth, not scale to $10M+.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Current customers have retention rate of 80-90%+ per year
Revenue goal is moderate (e.g., doubling to $250K/month), not 10-20x scale
Current channel can absorb 3x volume increase
claims.mechanism: High retention means each new customer stacks on existing base permanently; frequency increases compound the stack without requiring new customer acquisition infrastructure changes.

numbers.axis: viable revenue goal range by growth path

anchors.region: Staying with low-value segment + tripling outreach

bounded_by: Does not apply if the lower-value segment market is too thin to support 10x outreach volume

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that list segmentation and list enrichment (identifying prospect characteristics that predict high-value customers before outreach) are inherent parts of effective cold outreach — not a bug or anomaly — and that receiving a mix of high and low-value leads is expected and does not invalidate the channel.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Cold outbound lead generation via scraping and direct outreach
B2B markets with high variance in customer LTV within a single industry vertical

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when pivoting to a new, higher-value customer segment, the correct test is whether new customers reorder (revenue retention), and confirming reordering as quickly as possible is the primary validation gate before committing resources to scaling the new segment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business testing a new customer segment with unknown retention characteristics
Existing business model already working in a different segment
claims.mechanism: Revenue retention (reorders) determines whether the new segment will stack compounding revenue or require constant replacement of one-time buyers; without it, CAC never pays off and the business cannot scale.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when testing a new customer segment, the correct approach is to build a parallel acquisition channel rather than shutting down the existing business; the existing channel should continue operating via an operator while the founder focuses on the new segment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business already generating reliable recurring revenue from an existing segment
Founder testing a new, potentially higher-value segment
bounded_by: Does not mean building many verticals simultaneously — commit to one new segment only

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that committing to a single new customer vertical is essential when expanding; having multiple verticals in parallel means relearning acquisition, nuances, and sales for each one independently, multiplying the knowledge cost without increasing the probability of success on any single one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder-led business without dedicated vertical sales teams
claims.mechanism: Each new vertical has unique acquisition channels, prospect nuances, and sales processes; the learning overhead accumulates multiplicatively across verticals, whereas focusing on one allows that learning to compound.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a middleman business with essentially fixed delivery operations, switching to a larger-order customer segment does not require relearning the delivery side — only the acquisition side (how to find and convert the new customer) needs to be solved, making the operational risk of the pivot lower than it appears.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: True middleman business: design and coordination are fixed activities; manufacturing is outsourced regardless of order size
claims.mechanism: Outsourced manufacturing scales with order size without changing the middleman's operational model; therefore the cost structure and delivery process are effectively identical at 50 shirts or 5,000 shirts, making segment-switching purely an acquisition challenge.
bounded_by: Does not apply to vertically integrated businesses where manufacturing overhead would change with order size

examples.text: McKenzie runs a custom apparel business at $100K/month top-line revenue with 35% gross margins. His primary customer base is college organizations (fraternities, sororities) averaging $1,200-$1,500 per year in spend. He also has customers in construction and summer camps who spend up to $50,000 per year, but he has not focused acquisition on those segments because he cannot reliably identify which construction companies will be high-spend versus low-spend before reaching out. Alex Hormozi advises him that the 25-100x difference in customer value makes the higher-value segments worth pursuing despite the qualification challenge, and that the key validation test for the new segment is whether those customers reorder.

When McKenzie raises the concern that his cold outreach to construction companies produces a mix of companies that spend nothing and companies that spend $50,000/year, Hormozi reframes this as a normal feature of outbound lead generation rather than a disqualifying problem. He describes this situation as 'list segmentation and list enrichment' being part of effective outreach, implying that the qualification work is expected overhead, not a signal that the channel is broken.

Hormozi presents a concrete numerical comparison to illustrate why margin percentage is the wrong north star for a middleman: 50 shirts at 50% gross margin versus 5,000 shirts at 20% gross margin. In absolute dollar terms, 5,000 shirts at 20% is vastly more profitable, yet measuring success by margin percentage would make the 50-shirt order look superior. For an outsourced middleman, operational effort per order does not scale proportionally with order size, so the larger order is strictly better regardless of the lower margin rate.

Hormozi explicitly acknowledges that advising McKenzie to switch to a new customer segment (construction) before exhausting the college market violates his standard More/Better/New rule. He explains the override conditions: the order value difference is roughly 100x (1,500 vs. 50,000+ per year), the operational process is identical, and the college market cannot absorb 10-50x outreach volume. He frames the new segment as a test, not an irreversible commitment: 'If you do it and you just fall flat on your face... you can always just go back to the college.'

practices.text: When testing a new, higher-value customer segment, validate revenue retention (reorders) as quickly as possible before committing to scaling acquisition for that segment.

Build separate acquisition channels or websites for distinct customer avatars rather than serving all verticals from a single brand presence, but commit to one new vertical at a time rather than multiple simultaneously.
Use absolute gross profit per order (not gross margin percentage) as the primary filter when comparing customer segments in a middleman or outsourced-manufacturing business.
Leave an operator running the existing business when pivoting founder attention to a new, potentially higher-value customer segment so the existing revenue base continues compounding.
